Findings.Description: The acceptance criterion for CountWords("  leading and trailing  ") gives an incorrect expected result. The input contains three maximal contiguous letter/digit runs — "leading", "and", "trailing" — separated by whitespace, so per the spec's own word definition the correct count is 3, not 2.
Findings.Evidence: "CountWords(\"  leading and trailing  \") returns 2." versus the normative rule: "A word is defined as a maximal contiguous sequence of one or more characters that are letters or digits" and "Any character that is not a letter or digit ... acts as a separator".
Findings.Recommendation: Correct the expected value to 3, and re-verify all other acceptance-criteria examples by hand before they are used to derive automated tests.

Findings.Description: The specification does not settle whether 'letter or digit' means the Unicode general category (via char.IsLetterOrDigit) or strictly ASCII [a-zA-Z0-9]. This is flagged as an open question with a stated default assumption, but no acceptance criteria exercise non-ASCII input, so it does not block generation of the currently listed tests.
Findings.Evidence: OpenQuestions: "Does 'letters or digits' mean Unicode letters/digits ... or strictly ASCII? Assumption: Unicode letters/digits via char.IsLetterOrDigit, unless specified otherwise."
Findings.Recommendation: Confirm the Unicode-vs-ASCII decision with the requirement owner before implementing, and add explicit acceptance criteria/tests covering at least one non-ASCII letter/digit case (e.g., accented letters, non-Latin digits) once decided.

Summary: The specification is largely faithful to the original requirement (class/namespace/method shape, null/empty/whitespace handling, word definition) and most concrete examples check out arithmetically. However, one acceptance-criterion example — CountWords("  leading and trailing  ") returning 2 — is arithmetically wrong given the stated word definition (correct answer is 3), which is a blocking contradiction that would propagate an incorrect test into downstream work. A secondary, non-blocking ambiguity remains around Unicode vs. ASCII letter/digit classification, already surfaced as an open question with a reasonable default assumption.
